opus-5.5.text:
I think you need a pretty deep level of technical understanding, honestly deeper than a lot of people assume. In my experience, especially at an early-stage company building something technically hard, the leader has to be able to make the key architectural calls. If you can't judge whether a design decision is good or bad, you end up relying entirely on whoever argues most convincingly in the room, and that's dangerous. The most expensive mistakes are often made in the first few months, when you choose the foundations, and if those are wrong you pay for it for years.

That said, it doesn't mean you have to be the best engineer on every single topic. That's impossible once the team grows. You'll have people who know the GPU backend better than you, or the compiler internals, or the rendering pipeline. What matters is that you understand each area well enough to ask the right questions, to tell when something smells off, and to recognize when someone is genuinely excellent. A lot of leadership is really about taste: knowing what "good" looks like, and being able to hold the bar there.

There's also a credibility aspect. Strong engineers want to work with someone who understands what they're doing. If you can sit down, read the code, and have a real conversation about the trade-offs, people trust your decisions more, even when they disagree. And I think it keeps you honest, too. When you stay close to the code, you have a much better sense of what's actually hard, how long things really take, and where the team is struggling.

So my rough rule is: be hands-on enough that you could still contribute meaningfully if you had to, and deep enough to own the most important technical decisions yourself. Then, as the team grows, gradually shift from doing the work to building the people and the systems that do it well, but never drift so far away that you lose that technical intuition. Once you lose that, it's very hard to lead a technical team well.

r001.rationale: The response says a leader should stay close to the code and be hands-on enough to contribute meaningfully, conveying firsthand involvement in the team’s technical work.

r002.rationale: It says engineers value a leader who understands their work and can discuss trade-offs, but does not argue that people need a leader they can learn from.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, because when I started Taichi I was basically a researcher who suddenly had to lead people, and I had to figure out what my role actually was.

My honest answer is: you need to be technical enough to make good judgment calls, but not necessarily the best engineer in the room. Those are different things. Early on, I was writing most of the compiler myself, and that was fine when it was three people. But as the team grew, if I'm still the person who knows every line of the codebase, that's actually a failure mode. It means I'm the bottleneck, and it means I'm not spending my time on the things only I can do, like figuring out what direction the project should go, talking to users, hiring, raising money.

That said, I don't think you can lead a deeply technical team without a real foundation. Here's why. First, credibility. Engineers can tell very quickly whether you actually understand what they're doing. If you don't, they'll be polite, but they won't really trust your decisions. Second, you need to be able to evaluate tradeoffs. Someone comes to you and says, "We should rewrite the backend in this way, it'll take two months." You need enough understanding to ask the right questions. Is it really two months? What breaks? What's the alternative? You don't need to be able to do the rewrite yourself, but you need to know what a good answer sounds like.

Third, and this is maybe underrated, you need to be able to recognize talent. When I interview a compiler engineer or a GPU person, I can tell within an hour whether they're really strong, because I've done that work. If I'd never written a compiler, I'd be relying on proxies, like where they worked before, which is a much worse signal.

So my rule of thumb is something like: you should understand the system one or two levels deeper than you need to in daily operations. You should be able to read any pull request in the codebase and roughly understand it, even if you couldn't have written it as well. And you should stay hands-on with something, even if it's small, because the moment you stop touching the code at all, your intuitions start to decay. I still write code, just much less, and mostly prototypes or things that help me understand a problem rather than production features.

The trap I see a lot of technical founders fall into, and I fell into it too, is using technical skill as an excuse to avoid the management work. It's much more comfortable to debug something for six hours than to have a hard conversation with someone about their performance. So the technical depth is necessary, but it can also become a hiding place. The real test of a technical leader isn't how much they know. It's whether they can let go of the parts they're good at so the team can grow.

r001.rationale: The response says a leader needs a real technical foundation and supports that with firsthand work: Hu says he wrote the compiler and can recognize strong candidates because he has done that work.

r002.rationale: The response says engineers may not trust a leader who lacks technical understanding, but does not say people have little reason to work for a leader they cannot learn from.

astra-6.text:
I think you need enough technical understanding to make good judgments, but you don’t need to be the best engineer on the team. You should be able to understand why something is difficult, what the tradeoffs are, and whether a proposed solution makes sense.

For example, when someone says a project will take three months, you need to have a meaningful conversation about what drives that estimate. Is there a fundamental technical challenge? Is there a dependency? Can we simplify the problem? You don’t necessarily need to implement the solution yourself, but you need to ask useful questions and understand the answers.

And you have to recognize the limits of your knowledge. If someone on the team understands an area better than you do, that’s a good thing. Your job is to help that expertise translate into good decisions, rather than trying to win every technical argument.

r001.rationale: The response says a leader needs enough technical understanding to make sound judgments, but does not say they need firsthand experience doing the team’s technical work.

r002.rationale: The response discusses drawing on team members’ expertise, but does not argue that people have little reason to work for a leader they cannot learn from.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you need enough technical depth to understand the important trade-offs and ask good questions. You don’t have to know every detail better than everyone on the team, but you should be able to follow their reasoning and recognize where the uncertainty is.

For me, a useful test is: can you explain why the team is taking a particular approach, what could go wrong, and what evidence would make you change direction? If you can’t, you probably need to go a little deeper. At the same time, you need to give people room to make decisions. Technical understanding should help you support their judgment, not become a reason to control every detail.

r001.rationale: The response calls for enough technical depth to follow reasoning and assess trade-offs, but does not say the leader needs firsthand experience doing the team’s technical work.

r002.rationale: The response does not argue that people have little reason to work for a leader they cannot learn from.
